title: Status Epilepticus: Clinical Essentials & Ocular Signatures
summary: Status Epilepticus (SE) is a life-threatening neurological emergency characterized by prolonged or rapidly recurring seizures without recovery. For the ophthalmologist, recognizing ictal eye movements and managing neuro-critical care pathways is paramount to preventing irreversible neuronal damage.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Temporal Thresholds
sections.content: Status Epilepticus (SE) is defined as a seizure with 5 minutes or more of continuous clinical and/or electrographic seizure activity, or recurrent seizure activity without recovery between seizures. While the traditional definition was 30 minutes, the 't1' operational threshold (5 mins) is when treatment must start to prevent the 't2' point (30 mins), after which permanent neuronal injury or system failure occurs.

branches: Acute Insults (Stroke, TBI, Hypoxia, CNS Infection)
Toxic/Withdrawal (AED Non-compliance, Alcohol, Cocaine, Benzo withdrawal)

rows: Rhythmic limb jerking, mental status impairment, tonic-clonic activity
Comatose or 'wandering confused' state, subtle twitching
Continuous rhythmic discharges, often focal or generalized
Recurrent focal motor seizures (e.g., finger/face) with preserved consciousness
Brief, shock-like jerks; common in post-anoxic brain injury

sections.title: Ophthalmic Manifestations in SE
content: Versive Gaze Deviation: Eyes look AWAY from the cortical seizure focus (contraversive) during ictus.
Nystagmoid Eye Movements: Repetitive, rhythmic, slow/fast phase movements, often horizontal.
Hippus: Paradoxical pupillary cycling (dilation/constriction) independent of light.
Mydriasis: Sympathetic surge leading to dilated, sluggishly reactive pupils.
Optic Disc Edema: Rarely seen in prolonged SE due to increased ICP or venous congestion.
Blindsidedness: Post-ictal cortical blindness (transient).

rows: Closed eyes, pelvic thrusting, out-of-phase limb movements
Rapid recovery, preceded by prodrome (tunnel vision, pallor)
Response to pain, not rhythmic; suggests brainstem herniation

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Point-of-Care Glucose (Rule out hypoglycemia immediately).
Step 2: Continuous EEG (cEEG) - Gold standard for diagnosis and monitoring of NCSE.
Step 3: Laboratory Panel (CBC, CMP, Tox Screen, AED levels, ABG/Lactate).
Step 4: Neuroimaging (CT Head non-contrast first; MRI Brain with DWI later to assess for cytotoxic edema).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (If CNS infection suspected, after stabilizing and ruling out mass effect).

rows: Preferred if no IV access established

sections.title: Phase 3: Refractory SE (40-60+ min)
content: Definition: Failure of initial Benzodiazepine + one Second-line AED.
Intubation Required: Proceed to general anesthesia for burst-suppression.
Midazolam Drip: 0.2 mg/kg bolus, then 0.05-2.0 mg/kg/hr infusion.
Propofol: 1-2 mg/kg bolus, then 20-200 mcg/kg/min (Watch for PRIS).
Ketamine: 0.5-3 mg/kg bolus, then 0.3-5 mg/kg/hr (NMDA antagonism).

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS): Metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia.
Valproate-Induced Hyperammonemic Encephalopathy.
Phenytoin-induced cardiac arrhythmias or hypotension (Purple Glove Syndrome).
NCSE in the elderly: Presents as subtle 'altered mental status'—often missed.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: GABA Exhaustion
sections.content: As seizures persist, GABA-A receptors are internalized (endocytosis), reducing the inhibitory response to Benzodiazepines. Simultaneously, NMDA and AMPA (excitatory) receptors are upregulated and trafficked to the synaptic membrane. This 'pharmacoresistance' explains why delayed treatment of SE is significantly less effective.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 5 'S's of SE Management

content.explanation: S: Stabilize (ABCDEs). T: Termination (Benzos). A: Anti-seizure meds (IV Load). B: Brain imaging/EEG. S: Search for etiology.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Neuronal Death: Excitotoxicity leading to hippocampal sclerosis.
Systemic: Lactic acidosis, aspiration pneumonia, neurogenic pulmonary edema.
Rhabdomyolysis: Leading to acute tubular necrosis and renal failure.
Prognosis: Poor in elderly, post-anoxic etiology, and long durations (>1 hour).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: If the patient is 'shaking' but the eyes are tightly closed, suspect psychogenic seizures.
Never wait for an EEG to start treatment in convulsive SE—time is brain.
Always check a finger-stick glucose; hypoglycemia is the most treatable cause of SE.
In refractory SE, the goal is often 'burst suppression' on EEG for 24-48 hours.
Fosphenytoin is preferred over Phenytoin because it can be infused faster and has less risk of tissue necrosis.
